  • A ball thrown up always falls back down
  • Everything has weight because gravity pulls it
  • On the Moon, gravity is weaker — you'd weigh 6x less

lessons.title: Magnets
lessons.content:
Magnets

Learning Objectives

  • Describe the poles of a magnet
  • Explain attraction and repulsion
  • Identify magnetic and non-magnetic materials

1. Poles and Force

Every magnet has a north and south pole. Opposite poles attract; same poles repel.

Examples:

  • N + S = attract (pull together)
  • N + N = repel (push apart)
  • Earth is like a giant magnet with north and south magnetic poles

2. Magnetic Materials

Magnets attract some materials but not others.

Examples:

  • Magnetic: iron, steel, nickel, cobalt
  • Non-magnetic: wood, plastic, aluminum, glass
  • Paper clips stick to a magnet; pennies do not

lessons.title: The Solar System
lessons.content:
The Solar System

Learning Objectives

  • Name the 8 planets in order
  • Describe the role of the sun
  • Compare the sizes and features of planets

1. Our Solar System

The solar system includes the sun and everything that orbits it.

Examples:

  • 8 planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
  • My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Nachos (mnemonic)
  • Planets closer to the sun are usually warmer

2. Comparing Planets

Each planet has unique features.

Examples:

  • Jupiter: largest planet, has a giant storm (Great Red Spot)
  • Saturn: famous for its beautiful rings made of ice and rock
  • Mars: the Red Planet, has the tallest volcano in the solar system

lessons.title: Scientists and Science Tools
lessons.content:
Scientists and Science Tools

Learning Objectives

  • Describe the steps of the scientific method
  • Identify common science tools and their uses
  • Design a simple experiment

1. The Scientific Method

Scientists follow a process to answer questions.

Examples:

  • 1. Ask a question
  • 2. Make a hypothesis (prediction)
  • 3. Experiment/Observe
  • 4. Record data
  • 5. Draw a conclusion

2. Science Tools

Scientists use tools to observe and measure.

Examples:

  • Magnifying glass: see small details
  • Ruler/measuring tape: measure length
  • Thermometer: measure temperature
  • Balance scale: measure mass
  • Beaker/graduated cylinder: measure liquid volume

courses.title: Science — 3rd Grade
courses.description: Life, earth, physical science & more. Grade level: 3rd Grade.

lessons.title: Adaptations and Natural Selection
lessons.content:
Adaptations and Natural Selection

Learning Objectives

  • Define adaptation
  • Give examples of structural and behavioral adaptations
  • Explain how adaptations help survival

1. Structural Adaptations

Physical features that help an organism survive in its environment.

Examples:

  • Polar bear: thick fur and fat for insulation in the Arctic
  • Cactus: thick stem stores water in the desert
  • Duck: waterproof feathers keep it dry while swimming

2. Behavioral Adaptations

Actions that help an organism survive.

Examples:

  • Migration: monarch butterflies travel thousands of miles to stay warm
  • Hibernation: bears sleep through winter when food is scarce
  • Camouflage: stick insects look like twigs to avoid predators

lessons.title: Ecosystems and Biodiversity
lessons.content:
Ecosystems and Biodiversity

Learning Objectives

  • Define biodiversity and explain why it matters
  • Compare and contrast two ecosystems
  • Describe the impact of losing species from an ecosystem

1. What is Biodiversity?

Biodiversity refers to the variety of life in a particular area.

Examples:

  • A rainforest has millions of species of plants, animals, and insects
  • A monoculture farm (one crop only) has very low biodiversity
  • Higher biodiversity = healthier, more resilient ecosystem

2. Ecosystem Comparison

Different ecosystems support different communities of life.

Examples:

  • Coral reef: warm, shallow ocean water; home to fish, coral, turtles
  • Temperate forest: four seasons; home to deer, squirrels, woodpeckers, oaks

lessons.title: The Rock Cycle
lessons.content:
The Rock Cycle

Learning Objectives

  • Identify igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks
  • Explain how each type forms
  • Describe the rock cycle

1. Three Types of Rocks

Rocks form in different ways and can change from one type to another.

Examples:

  • Igneous: cooled magma — granite, basalt, obsidian
  • Sedimentary: layers of compressed sediment — sandstone, limestone, shale
  • Metamorphic: changed by heat and pressure — marble, slate, quartzite

2. The Rock Cycle

Rocks continuously change from one type to another over millions of years.

Examples:

  • Magma cools → igneous → weathering/erosion → sediment → pressure → sedimentary → heat/pressure → metamorphic → melt → magma

lessons.title: Weather, Water Cycle, and Climate
lessons.content:
Weather, Water Cycle, and Climate

Learning Objectives

  • Explain all four stages of the water cycle in detail
  • Describe how the water cycle affects weather
  • Define climate zones

1. Water Cycle in Depth

The water cycle continuously moves water between Earth's surface and atmosphere.

Examples:

  • Evaporation: sun heats water → rises as vapor
  • Transpiration: plants release water vapor
  • Condensation: vapor cools → forms clouds
  • Precipitation: rain, snow, sleet, hail falls

2. Climate Zones

Earth has different climate zones based on distance from the equator.

Examples:

  • Tropical (near equator): hot and humid all year
  • Temperate (mid latitudes): four distinct seasons
  • Polar (near poles): cold most of the year

lessons.title: Energy: Forms and Transformations
lessons.content:
Energy: Forms and Transformations

Learning Objectives

  • Name forms of energy: thermal, light, sound, electrical, mechanical
  • Explain energy transformation with examples
  • Describe how we generate and use energy

1. Forms of Energy

Energy exists in many forms and makes things happen.

Examples:

  • Thermal: heat from a fire or the sun
  • Light: sunlight or a lamp
  • Sound: music, thunder, talking
  • Electrical: powers lights and electronics
  • Mechanical: movement of a ball or bicycle

2. Energy Transformations

Energy changes from one form to another.

Examples:

  • Toaster: electrical → thermal (heat)
  • Solar panel: light → electrical
  • Drumming: mechanical → sound
  • Plants: light → chemical energy (photosynthesis)

lessons.title: Forces and Newton's Laws (Intro)
lessons.content:
Forces and Newton's Laws (Intro)

Learning Objectives

  • Explain balanced and unbalanced forces
  • Describe Newton's 1st Law (inertia)
  • Describe Newton's 3rd Law (action-reaction)

1. Balanced and Unbalanced Forces

When forces are balanced, objects stay still or keep moving. When unbalanced, motion changes.

Examples:

  • Tug of war — equal teams = balanced (no movement)
  • One team stronger = unbalanced (rope moves their way)
  • A book on a table: gravity pulls down, table pushes up — balanced!

2. Action-Reaction

For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

Examples:

  • Jump off a diving board — you push the board, the board pushes you up
  • A rocket expels gas downward — the gas pushes the rocket upward

lessons.title: Human Body: Organs and Systems
lessons.content:
Human Body: Organs and Systems

Learning Objectives

  • Name and locate major organs
  • Describe the function of key body systems
  • Explain how systems interact

1. Major Organs

Organs are structures in the body that do specific jobs.

Examples:

  • Brain: controls thinking, movement, and senses
  • Heart: pumps blood throughout the body
  • Lungs: take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide
  • Stomach: breaks down food

2. Body Systems

Organs work together in systems.

Examples:

  • Circulatory system: heart + blood vessels + blood
  • Digestive system: mouth → esophagus → stomach → intestines
  • Respiratory system: nose/mouth → trachea → lungs

lessons.title: Soil, Erosion, and Landforms
lessons.content:
Soil, Erosion, and Landforms

Learning Objectives

  • Define erosion and deposition
  • Explain how rivers carve canyons and form deltas
  • Describe how humans prevent erosion

1. Erosion and Deposition

Weathering breaks rocks apart. Erosion moves them. Deposition drops them somewhere new.

Examples:

  • A river erodes its banks over time, carving canyons
  • The Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon over millions of years
  • River delta: sediment deposited where river meets sea

2. Preventing Erosion

Humans can slow erosion to protect farmland and coastlines.

Examples:

  • Planting trees: roots hold soil in place
  • Terracing: step-like farming on hillsides
  • Seawalls: protect coastlines from wave erosion

lessons.title: Electricity and Circuits
lessons.content:
Electricity and Circuits

Learning Objectives

  • Explain static electricity
  • Describe a complete circuit
  • Distinguish conductors from insulators

1. Static Electricity

Static electricity is a buildup of electric charge on a surface.

Examples:

  • Rub a balloon on your hair — it sticks to the wall
  • Lightning is a giant static electricity discharge
  • Socks sticking together from the dryer

2. Circuits

A circuit is a closed path through which electricity flows.

Examples:

  • Complete circuit: battery → wire → light bulb → wire → battery (light turns on)
  • Broken circuit: gap in the wire = light stays off
  • Conductors: copper, iron, water
  • Insulators: plastic, rubber, wood

lessons.title: Science and Engineering Design
lessons.content:
Science and Engineering Design

Learning Objectives

  • Describe the engineering design process
  • Identify a problem and design a solution
  • Test, evaluate, and improve a design

1. Engineering Design Process

Engineers follow a process when designing solutions.

Examples:

  • 1. Define the problem
  • 2. Research and brainstorm solutions
  • 3. Design your solution (sketch it)
  • 4. Build a prototype
  • 5. Test and evaluate
  • 6. Improve and redesign

2. Real-World Engineering

Engineers solve problems all around us.

Examples:

  • Problem: bridges need to hold weight → engineers design suspension bridges
  • Problem: need clean water → engineers design filtration systems
  • Problem: need to communicate far away → engineers design satellites

courses.title: Science — 4th Grade
courses.description: Life, earth, physical science & more. Grade level: 4th Grade.

lessons.title: Structures of Life: Cells
lessons.content:
Structures of Life: Cells

Learning Objectives

  • Explain that all living things are made of cells
  • Identify key parts of a cell (cell membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm)
  • Compare plant and animal cells

1. The Cell: Basic Unit of Life

Cells are the tiny building blocks of all living things.

Examples:

  • A single bacterium is made of just one cell
  • The human body is made of about 37 trillion cells
  • Cells are too small to see without a microscope

2. Plant vs. Animal Cells

Both cell types share some structures, but plant cells have extra features.

Examples:

  • Shared: nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane
  • Plant only: cell wall (rigid support), chloroplasts (capture light), large central vacuole
  • Animal only: centrioles (help with cell division)

lessons.title: Ecosystems: Energy Flow and Food Webs
lessons.content:
Ecosystems: Energy Flow and Food Webs

Learning Objectives

  • Explain energy flow from sun to producers to consumers
  • Build and analyze a food web
  • Predict the impact of adding or removing a species

1. Energy Pyramids

Energy decreases as it moves up the food chain.

Examples:

  • Only about 10% of energy passes from one level to the next
  • Bottom level (plants) has the most energy; top predators have the least
  • This is why there are fewer tigers than deer

2. Keystone Species

Some species have an outsized effect on their ecosystem.

Examples:

  • Sea otters eat sea urchins; without otters, urchins overgraze kelp forests
  • Wolves in Yellowstone control deer populations, which allows trees to regrow
  • Remove a keystone species → ecosystem dramatically changes

lessons.title: Weather, Climate Change, and Human Impact
lessons.content:
Weather, Climate Change, and Human Impact

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the greenhouse effect
  • Describe how human activities contribute to climate change
  • Identify solutions and personal actions to reduce impact

1. The Greenhouse Effect

Greenhouse gases trap heat in Earth's atmosphere, like a blanket.

Examples:

  • Natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough for life
  • Too many greenhouse gases (CO₂, methane) trap extra heat
  • This causes global average temperatures to rise

2. Human Impact and Solutions

Human activities release greenhouse gases, but we can make changes.

Examples:

  • Burning fossil fuels for energy and transportation releases CO₂
  • Solutions: renewable energy (solar, wind), electric vehicles, planting forests
  • You can help: reduce energy use, eat less meat, walk or bike

lessons.title: Waves: Light and Sound
lessons.content:
Waves: Light and Sound

Learning Objectives

  • Describe wavelength, amplitude, and frequency
  • Explain how light is reflected, refracted, and absorbed
  • Explain how the ear detects sound waves

1. Wave Properties

Waves carry energy and have measurable properties.

Examples:

  • Wavelength: distance from one peak to the next
  • Amplitude: height of the wave (higher = louder sound or brighter light)
  • Frequency: how many waves pass per second (higher = higher pitch)

2. Light: Reflection and Refraction

Light behaves differently when it hits different surfaces.

Examples:

  • Reflection: mirror bounces light back
  • Refraction: light bends when passing through water or glass — this is why a straw looks bent in a cup
  • Absorption: dark surfaces absorb light; light surfaces reflect it

lessons.title: Electricity and Magnetism
lessons.content:
Electricity and Magnetism

Learning Objectives

  • Explain how an electromagnet works
  • Describe series and parallel circuits
  • Explore real-world uses of electromagnets

1. Electromagnets

Running electricity through a wire coil creates a magnetic field.

Examples:

  • Wrap wire around a nail, connect to a battery → nail becomes magnetic
  • Turn off the current → magnetism disappears
  • Strength increases with more wire coils or stronger battery

2. Series and Parallel Circuits

Circuits can be arranged in two ways.

Examples:

  • Series: one path — if one bulb goes out, all go out (old Christmas lights)
  • Parallel: multiple paths — if one bulb goes out, others stay on (home wiring)

lessons.title: Earth's History and Geologic Time
lessons.content:
Earth's History and Geologic Time

Learning Objectives

  • Describe Earth's formation approximately 4.6 billion years ago
  • Explain how fossils provide evidence of ancient life
  • Describe major events in Earth's history

1. Earth's Timeline

Earth has existed for about 4.6 billion years — an almost unimaginable amount of time.

Examples:

  • If Earth's history were compressed into 24 hours, humans would appear in the last 2 seconds
  • First life (simple cells): ~3.8 billion years ago
  • Dinosaurs: 230–65 million years ago

2. Fossils as Evidence

Fossils preserve clues about life that existed millions of years ago.

Examples:

  • Ammonite fossils found in mountains prove these areas were once underwater
  • Fossilized footprints show how dinosaurs moved
  • Scientists use the age of surrounding rock to date fossils

lessons.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
lessons.content:
Newton's Laws of Motion

Learning Objectives

  • State and explain Newton's 3 Laws
  • Apply each law to everyday examples
  • Calculate force using F = m × a (conceptually)

1. Newton's Three Laws

Three laws describe how objects move.

Examples:

  • Law 1 (Inertia): An object at rest stays at rest; an object in motion stays in motion unless a force acts on it.
  • Law 2 (F = ma): More force = more acceleration; heavier objects need more force to move.
  • Law 3 (Action-Reaction): For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.

2. Laws in Real Life

Newton's Laws explain everyday movement.

Examples:

  • Law 1: You lurch forward when a car brakes suddenly (your body wants to keep moving)
  • Law 2: Pushing a shopping cart vs. a car — same force, different acceleration
  • Law 3: A swimmer pushes water back, water pushes the swimmer forward

lessons.title: The Solar System and Space Exploration
lessons.content:
The Solar System and Space Exploration

Learning Objectives

  • Describe the sun, planets, asteroids, and comets
  • Explain gravity's role in keeping planets in orbit
  • Describe key milestones in space exploration

1. Solar System in Depth

The solar system is held together by the sun's gravity.

Examples:

  • Inner planets (rocky): Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars
  • Outer planets (gas giants): Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
  • Asteroid belt: between Mars and Jupiter
  • Comets: icy bodies with tails of gas and dust

2. Space Exploration

Humans have explored space with rockets, satellites, and rovers.

Examples:

  • 1957: Sputnik — first satellite in orbit
  • 1969: Apollo 11 — first humans on the Moon
  • 2004–present: Mars rovers (Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, Perseverance)
  • James Webb Space Telescope: sees farther than ever before

lessons.title: Human Body: Nutrition and Health
lessons.content:
Human Body: Nutrition and Health

Learning Objectives

  • Identify the six classes of nutrients
  • Explain the role of each nutrient in the body
  • Evaluate the health benefits of food and activity choices

1. Six Nutrients

The body needs six types of nutrients to function.

Examples:

  • Carbohydrates: main energy source (bread, rice, fruit)
  • Proteins: build and repair tissue (meat, beans, eggs)
  • Fats: store energy and protect organs (nuts, oils, avocado)
  • Vitamins: support body processes (C, D, B12...)
  • Minerals: build bones and carry oxygen (calcium, iron, potassium)
  • Water: makes up ~60% of the body and supports every process

2. Healthy Habits

Food choices and physical activity affect long-term health.

Examples:

  • Exercise strengthens the heart and muscles
  • Sleep allows the brain to consolidate memories and the body to repair
  • Fruits and vegetables provide vitamins, minerals, and fiber

lessons.title: Engineering Design and Innovation
lessons.content:
Engineering Design and Innovation

Learning Objectives

  • Refine the engineering design process with criteria and constraints
  • Compare and test multiple design solutions
  • Communicate and present design findings

1. Criteria and Constraints

Every engineering challenge has criteria (what the design must do) and constraints (limits).

Examples:

  • Bridge challenge: must hold 500g (criteria); can only use 20 popsicle sticks and tape (constraints)
  • Real-world: a car must be safe and affordable; engineers can't use unlimited materials or time

2. Testing and Presenting Solutions

Engineers test designs, collect data, and communicate results.

Examples:

  • Test your bridge with increasing weights and record when it fails
  • Graph the data: which design held the most weight?
  • Present: explain your design, what worked, what you'd change

courses.title: History — Kindergarten
courses.description: World & American history across the ages. Grade level: Kindergarten.

lessons.title: My Family History
lessons.content:
My Family History

Learning Objectives

  • Describe their own family
  • Compare families across cultures
  • Understand that families have histories and traditions

1. All Kinds of Families

Families come in many shapes and sizes, but all families care for one another.

Examples:

  • Some families have two parents, some have one
  • Some children live with grandparents or aunts and uncles
  • Families can have many kids or just one

2. Family Traditions

Traditions are special things families do together, often passed down through generations.

Examples:

  • Holiday celebrations and foods
  • Bedtime stories or weekend rituals
  • Cultural dances, songs, or clothing

lessons.title: Classroom and School Community
lessons.content:
Classroom and School Community

Learning Objectives

  • Define community
  • Identify classroom rules and why they exist
  • Explain the roles of people in a school

1. Our Classroom Community

A community is a group of people who live or work together and help each other.

Examples:

  • The classroom is a small community
  • Rules help everyone feel safe and respected
  • Everyone has a job: student, teacher, principal, custodian

2. Rights and Responsibilities

In a community, everyone has rights (what they deserve) and responsibilities (what they must do).

Examples:

  • Right: to be heard; Responsibility: to listen to others
  • Right: to learn; Responsibility: to follow classroom rules

lessons.title: Holidays and Celebrations
lessons.content:
Holidays and Celebrations

Learning Objectives

  • Name important national holidays
  • Explain why holidays are celebrated
  • Connect holidays to community values

1. National Holidays

National holidays honor important events and people in a country's history.

Examples:

  • Independence Day: celebrates when the U.S. declared independence
  • Thanksgiving: a time to be grateful and share with others
  • Martin Luther King Jr. Day: honors a leader who fought for equality

2. Cultural Celebrations

Different cultures have their own celebrations that bring communities together.

Examples:

  • Lunar New Year celebrated in many Asian cultures
  • Diwali: the Hindu festival of lights
  • Hanukkah: Jewish festival of lights

lessons.title: People Who Help Us — Community Heroes
lessons.content:
People Who Help Us — Community Heroes

Learning Objectives

  • Identify community helpers (firefighters, doctors, teachers)
  • Explain how helpers make communities safer
  • Name historical figures who helped others

1. Community Helpers Today

Community helpers keep neighborhoods safe, healthy, and running smoothly.

Examples:

  • Firefighters put out fires and rescue people
  • Doctors and nurses keep people healthy
  • Teachers help children learn

2. Heroes from History

Throughout history, people have done brave things to help others.

Examples:

  • Harriet Tubman helped enslaved people escape to freedom
  • Florence Nightingale improved hospital care for soldiers
  • Fred Rogers made children feel valued and loved

lessons.title: Then and Now — How Things Change
lessons.content:
Then and Now — How Things Change

Learning Objectives

  • Compare old and new versions of everyday items
  • Use vocabulary: past, present, change
  • Understand that history shows how things change over time

1. Transportation Then and Now

The ways people travel have changed greatly over time.

Examples:

  • Then: horse and buggy, steam trains
  • Now: cars, airplanes, high-speed trains
  • Future: electric vehicles, possibly flying cars

2. Communication Then and Now

How people share information has transformed over centuries.

Examples:

  • Then: letters delivered by hand, town criers
  • Later: telegraph, telephone
  • Now: texting, video calls, social media

lessons.title: American Symbols and Landmarks
lessons.content:
American Symbols and Landmarks

Learning Objectives

  • Name major American symbols
  • Explain what the flag and Pledge represent
  • Identify famous national landmarks

1. American Symbols

Symbols represent ideas that are important to a nation.

Examples:

  • The American flag: 50 stars (states) and 13 stripes (original colonies)
  • The Bald Eagle: national bird symbolizing freedom and strength
  • The Liberty Bell: symbol of independence and freedom

2. Famous Landmarks

Landmarks are important places that represent the nation's history.

Examples:

  • Statue of Liberty: gift from France, welcomes immigrants
  • Mount Rushmore: carved faces of four presidents
  • The White House: where the President lives and works

lessons.title: Leaders and Government — A First Look
lessons.content:
Leaders and Government — A First Look

Learning Objectives

  • Explain why communities need leaders
  • Identify roles of a mayor, governor, and president (simply)
  • Understand that rules and laws help communities

1. Why We Need Leaders

Leaders help communities make decisions and stay organized.

Examples:

  • A class president organizes school events
  • A mayor makes decisions for a city
  • The President leads the whole country

2. Rules and Laws

Rules in school are like laws in a country — they help keep everyone safe and fair.

Examples:

  • School rule: walk in the hallways
  • City law: stop at a red light
  • National law: everyone deserves to be treated equally

lessons.title: Native Americans — First Peoples
lessons.content:
Native Americans — First Peoples

Learning Objectives

  • Name a few Native American tribes
  • Describe how Native peoples lived in harmony with nature
  • Show respect for diverse Indigenous cultures

1. Many Nations

Before European explorers arrived, hundreds of different Native nations lived across North America.

Examples:

  • Lakota Sioux: Plains hunters, lived in tipis
  • Pueblo peoples: Southwest farmers, built adobe homes
  • Iroquois: Northeast forest people, built longhouses

2. Living with Nature

Native peoples had deep knowledge of and respect for the natural world.

Examples:

  • Planted the Three Sisters: corn, beans, and squash together
  • Used every part of the buffalo: food, clothing, shelter
  • Passed down knowledge through oral storytelling

lessons.title: Explorers and Discovery
lessons.content:
Explorers and Discovery

Learning Objectives

  • Define exploration
  • Name one or two early explorers
  • Explain why people explore new places

1. What is Exploration?

Exploration means traveling to places that are new or unknown to discover what is there.

Examples:

  • Explorers travel to find new land, resources, or trade routes
  • Today, people explore space, the ocean floor, and remote jungles

2. Early Explorers

Long ago, brave sailors crossed oceans to explore new lands.

Examples:

  • Christopher Columbus sailed from Spain in 1492 and reached the Americas
  • Leif Erikson (Viking) may have reached North America even earlier
  • Exploration brought peoples from different worlds into contact

lessons.title: Looking Back — How We Learn History
lessons.content:
Looking Back — How We Learn History

Learning Objectives

  • Define history and historian
  • Distinguish between primary and secondary sources (simply)
  • Explain how artifacts help us understand the past

1. What Is History?

History is the story of what happened in the past. Historians are people who study it.

Examples:

  • We study history to understand where we came from
  • Knowing the past helps us make better decisions today

2. Sources and Artifacts

Historians use sources — clues from the past — to learn what happened.

Examples:

  • Primary source: a photo, diary, or letter from the time
  • Secondary source: a book or article written later about that time
  • Artifact: an old object like a tool, coin, or toy that tells a story

courses.title: History — 1st Grade
courses.description: World & American history across the ages. Grade level: 1st Grade.

lessons.title: Families and Communities Over Time
lessons.content:
Families and Communities Over Time

Learning Objectives

  • Compare family life across generations
  • Identify changes in community over time
  • Use timeline vocabulary: past, present, future

1. Generations

A generation is all the people born and living at about the same time.

Examples:

  • Your grandparents' generation grew up without smartphones
  • Your parents' generation saw the internet become widespread
  • Your generation has grown up with tablets and streaming

2. Community Changes

Communities change over time due to new people, technology, and events.

Examples:

  • A small farm town may grow into a city
  • New schools and hospitals are built as populations grow
  • Old buildings may be torn down or preserved as historical landmarks

lessons.title: American Heroes and Role Models
lessons.content:
American Heroes and Role Models

Learning Objectives

  • Name and describe at least three American heroes
  • Explain what made each person significant
  • Connect their values to present-day life

1. Abraham Lincoln

Lincoln led the country during the Civil War and helped end slavery.

Examples:

  • Born in a log cabin in Kentucky — rose from poverty to the presidency
  • Issued the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863, declaring enslaved people free
  • Famous quote: 'A house divided against itself cannot stand'

2. Rosa Parks and Civil Rights

Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in 1955, sparking the Montgomery Bus Boycott.

Examples:

  • Her action helped launch the modern Civil Rights Movement
  • She showed that one person's courage can change history
  • Martin Luther King Jr. led the boycott that followed

lessons.title: The First Americans
lessons.content:
The First Americans

Learning Objectives

  • Compare cultures of Native peoples from different regions
  • Describe how environment shaped Native lifestyles
  • Show respect for Indigenous history and traditions

1. Regional Cultures

Native American cultures varied greatly by region because of different environments.

Examples:

  • Pacific Northwest: abundant fish and forests; totem poles, cedar canoes
  • Great Plains: buffalo hunting; tipis, horse riding
  • Eastern Woodlands: farming and hunting; longhouses, wampum

2. Contributions and Legacy

Native Americans contributed many things to the world that we still use today.

Examples:

  • Foods: corn, potatoes, tomatoes, chocolate, squash
  • Place names: Mississippi, Ohio, Chicago, Manhattan
  • Agricultural techniques: companion planting, irrigation methods

lessons.title: Pilgrims and Early Settlements
lessons.content:
Pilgrims and Early Settlements

Learning Objectives

  • Explain why Pilgrims left England
  • Describe the Mayflower voyage
  • Explain the relationship between Pilgrims and the Wampanoag people

1. The Mayflower Voyage

In 1620, the Pilgrims sailed for 66 days across the Atlantic on the Mayflower.

Examples:

  • About 102 passengers, cramped and seasick
  • They arrived at Plymouth, Massachusetts in November — too late to plant crops
  • Half the colonists died the first winter from cold and hunger

2. Squanto and the Wampanoag

The Wampanoag people, led by Squanto and Chief Massasoit, helped the Pilgrims survive.

Examples:

  • Squanto taught Pilgrims to plant corn, fish, and find food
  • The harvest feast of 1621 is remembered as the first Thanksgiving
  • Early relations were cooperative, but later deteriorated as more colonists arrived

lessons.title: The American Revolution — A New Nation
lessons.content:
The American Revolution — A New Nation

Learning Objectives

  • Explain why colonists wanted independence
  • Name key figures: Washington, Jefferson, Franklin
  • Describe the significance of the Declaration of Independence

1. Why Colonists Rebelled

The colonists were angry about being taxed by Britain without having a say.

Examples:

  • 'No taxation without representation' was their rallying cry
  • The Boston Tea Party (1773): colonists dumped British tea into Boston Harbor to protest
  • British soldiers were quartered in colonists' homes against their will

2. Declaration of Independence

On July 4, 1776, leaders signed the Declaration of Independence.

Examples:

  • Written mainly by Thomas Jefferson
  • 'All men are created equal' — a revolutionary idea at the time
  • This document created the United States of America

lessons.title: The Constitution and Government
lessons.content:
The Constitution and Government

Learning Objectives

  • Explain why the Constitution was written
  • Name the three branches of government
  • Explain the concept of checks and balances

1. Why We Have a Constitution

After independence, America needed a set of rules for governing the new nation.

Examples:

  • The Constitution was written in 1787 in Philadelphia
  • It created a government strong enough to lead, but not so powerful it could become a dictatorship
  • The Bill of Rights (first 10 amendments) protects individual freedoms

2. Three Branches

The government is divided into three branches to share and balance power.

Examples:

  • Legislative (Congress): makes laws
  • Executive (President): carries out laws
  • Judicial (Supreme Court): interprets laws

lessons.title: Westward Expansion
lessons.content:
Westward Expansion

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the idea of Manifest Destiny
  • Describe life on the Oregon Trail
  • Discuss the impact on Native American communities

1. Moving West

In the 1800s, millions of Americans traveled west in covered wagons seeking land and opportunity.

Examples:

  • The Oregon Trail stretched 2,000 miles from Missouri to Oregon
  • Pioneers faced harsh weather, illness, and difficult terrain
  • Some were looking for gold (California Gold Rush, 1849)

2. Impact on Native Americans

Westward expansion devastated Native American communities.

Examples:

  • The Indian Removal Act forced Native peoples from their ancestral lands
  • The Trail of Tears: Cherokee Nation forced to march over 1,000 miles; thousands died
  • Buffalo herds were nearly wiped out, destroying the Plains peoples' way of life

lessons.title: The Civil War
lessons.content:
The Civil War

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the main cause of the Civil War (slavery)
  • Describe key figures: Lincoln, Frederick Douglass, Harriet Tubman
  • Explain what the Civil War changed

1. A Nation Divided

The Civil War (1861–1865) was fought between the Northern states (Union) and Southern states (Confederacy).

Examples:

  • The South depended on enslaved labor for its economy
  • Lincoln's election in 1860 triggered Southern states to secede
  • Over 600,000 soldiers died — the deadliest war in American history

2. Emancipation and Reconstruction

The Union's victory ended slavery and began Reconstruction.

Examples:

  • 13th Amendment (1865): abolished slavery
  • Frederick Douglass: escaped slavery and became a powerful speaker and abolitionist
  • Reconstruction tried to rebuild the South and integrate freed Black Americans into society

lessons.title: Immigration and the American Dream
lessons.content:
Immigration and the American Dream

Learning Objectives

  • Explain why people immigrate
  • Describe Ellis Island and Angel Island
  • Connect immigration to America's diverse culture

1. Why People Immigrate

Throughout history, people have come to America seeking safety, freedom, and opportunity.

Examples:

  • Irish fled the Great Famine of the 1840s
  • Eastern Europeans escaped poverty and persecution in the late 1800s–early 1900s
  • Today people still immigrate from Latin America, Asia, Africa, and elsewhere

2. Ellis Island and Angel Island

Millions of immigrants entered the U.S. through gateway stations.

Examples:

  • Ellis Island (New York): over 12 million Europeans passed through 1892–1954
  • Angel Island (San Francisco): gateway for Asian immigrants, often detained longer
  • Many changed their names upon arrival; others kept them as a sign of identity

lessons.title: The 20th Century — Change and Progress
lessons.content:
The 20th Century — Change and Progress

Learning Objectives

  • Name key events: World Wars, Civil Rights, moon landing
  • Explain how technology changed daily life
  • Describe the Civil Rights Movement and its achievements

1. Major Events

The 20th century brought enormous changes to America and the world.

Examples:

  • World War I (1914–1918) and World War II (1939–1945): global conflicts
  • The Great Depression (1930s): economic crisis affecting millions
  • Apollo 11 (1969): humans walked on the moon for the first time

2. The Civil Rights Movement

African Americans and allies fought for equal rights throughout the 20th century.

Examples:

  • Rosa Parks (1955), Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have a Dream' speech (1963)
  • March on Washington, Civil Rights Act (1964), Voting Rights Act (1965)
  • Barack Obama elected first Black U.S. president in 2008

courses.title: History — 2nd Grade
courses.description: World & American history across the ages. Grade level: 2nd Grade.

lessons.title: Ancient Civilizations — Mesopotamia
lessons.content:
Ancient Civilizations — Mesopotamia

Learning Objectives

  • Locate Mesopotamia on a map
  • Explain why civilization began between the Tigris and Euphrates
  • Describe major achievements: writing, cities, laws

1. The Fertile Crescent

Mesopotamia means 'land between the rivers' — located in modern-day Iraq.

Examples:

  • The Tigris and Euphrates rivers flooded, depositing rich soil for farming
  • Surplus food allowed people to specialize in other jobs: priests, soldiers, merchants
  • Sumer was the world's first known civilization (~3500 BCE)

2. Achievements

Mesopotamians made lasting contributions to human civilization.

Examples:

  • Cuneiform: earliest known writing system (wedge-shaped symbols on clay tablets)
  • The wheel: invented around 3500 BCE
  • Code of Hammurabi: one of the earliest written law codes (~1754 BCE)

lessons.title: Ancient Egypt
lessons.content:
Ancient Egypt

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the role of the Nile River
  • Describe Egyptian society and the role of pharaohs
  • Explain why and how the pyramids were built

1. Gift of the Nile

Egyptian civilization depended entirely on the Nile River.

Examples:

  • Annual floods deposited fertile black soil (called 'the gift of the Nile')
  • Egypt was divided into Upper and Lower Egypt, unified around 3100 BCE
  • The Nile also served as a highway for trade and communication

2. Pharaohs and Pyramids

Pharaohs were god-kings who ruled Egypt with absolute power.

Examples:

  • The Great Pyramid of Giza: built for Pharaoh Khufu ~2560 BCE
  • Built by tens of thousands of workers over 20 years
  • Hieroglyphics: Egyptian writing using pictures to represent words and sounds

lessons.title: Ancient Greece
lessons.content:
Ancient Greece

Learning Objectives

  • Explain how geography shaped Greek civilization
  • Describe the birth of democracy in Athens
  • Name key figures: Socrates, Aristotle, Alexander the Great

1. The Greek City-States

Greece was made up of independent city-states, each with its own government and culture.

Examples:

  • Athens: known for democracy, philosophy, and the arts
  • Sparta: known for its powerful military and disciplined warriors
  • Competition between city-states sometimes led to war (Peloponnesian War)

2. Democracy and Legacy

Ancient Greece gave the world democracy and laid the foundation for Western thought.

Examples:

  • Athenian democracy (~500 BCE): citizens voted on laws directly
  • Olympics: first held in Olympia in 776 BCE to honor the god Zeus
  • Greek philosophy (Socrates, Plato, Aristotle) still shapes education today

lessons.title: Ancient Rome
lessons.content:
Ancient Rome

Learning Objectives

  • Describe the transition from Roman Republic to Roman Empire
  • Explain Rome's contributions to law, language, and architecture
  • Describe the fall of Rome and its causes

1. Republic to Empire

Rome began as a republic governed by elected officials, then became an empire under Julius Caesar and Augustus.

Examples:

  • Roman Senate: elected leaders made laws (like a congress)
  • Julius Caesar gained enormous power; was assassinated in 44 BCE
  • Augustus became the first Emperor of Rome in 27 BCE

2. Roman Legacy

Rome's influence is everywhere in the modern world.

Examples:

  • Latin: basis for Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese, and much English vocabulary
  • Roman law: foundation of modern legal systems in many countries
  • Roman engineering: concrete, aqueducts, roads, arches — many still stand today

lessons.title: The Middle Ages
lessons.content:
The Middle Ages

Learning Objectives

  • Describe the feudal system
  • Explain the role of castles and knights
  • Describe the importance of the Church in medieval life

1. Feudalism

Medieval society was organized in a strict hierarchy called feudalism.

Examples:

  • King → Nobles → Knights → Peasants/Serfs
  • Peasants farmed the land and gave a portion to their lord in exchange for protection
  • Most people were born into their social class and could not easily leave it

2. Castles and the Church

Castles provided military defense; the Church provided spiritual and community guidance.

Examples:

  • Castles had moats, drawbridges, towers, and thick walls
  • Knights followed a code of chivalry: courage, honor, and service to the weak
  • The Catholic Church ran schools, hospitals, and collected taxes; the Pope was extremely powerful

lessons.title: The Renaissance
lessons.content:
The Renaissance

Learning Objectives

  • Explain what the Renaissance was and why it began
  • Name key Renaissance figures in art and science
  • Connect Renaissance ideas to the modern world

1. Rebirth of Ideas

The Renaissance (meaning 'rebirth') began in Italy around 1300 and spread across Europe.

Examples:

  • After the Middle Ages, people rediscovered ancient Greek and Roman knowledge
  • Wealthy families (like the Medici in Florence) funded artists and scholars
  • The printing press (Gutenberg, ~1440) made books affordable and spread new ideas rapidly

2. Great Thinkers and Artists

The Renaissance produced some of history's greatest minds.

Examples:

  • Leonardo da Vinci: Mona Lisa, The Last Supper, anatomical drawings, inventions
  • Michelangelo: Sistine Chapel ceiling, sculpture of David
  • Galileo Galilei: proved Earth orbits the sun (heliocentric model), improved the telescope

lessons.title: Age of Exploration
lessons.content:
Age of Exploration

Learning Objectives

  • Name key explorers and their routes
  • Explain motivations for exploration (gold, glory, God)
  • Describe the Columbian Exchange and its impact

1. Why Europeans Explored

Europeans sailed to find new trade routes, wealth, and to spread Christianity.

Examples:

  • Columbus (1492): reached the Caribbean seeking a route to Asia
  • Vasco da Gama (1498): first European to sail around Africa to India
  • Magellan's crew (1519–1522): first to circumnavigate the globe

2. The Columbian Exchange

The contact between Europe and the Americas triggered a massive exchange of goods, people, and diseases.

Examples:

  • Europe to Americas: horses, cattle, wheat, smallpox (devastating to Native peoples)
  • Americas to Europe: potatoes, corn, tomatoes, chocolate, tobacco
  • Millions of Native Americans died from diseases to which they had no immunity

lessons.title: The Industrial Revolution
lessons.content:
The Industrial Revolution

Learning Objectives

  • Explain how the Industrial Revolution began
  • Describe how factories changed work and family life
  • Identify key inventions and inventors

1. From Farm to Factory

Beginning in Britain in the late 1700s, machines began replacing hand tools in manufacturing.

Examples:

  • Steam engine (James Watt, 1769): powered factories, trains, and ships
  • Spinning jenny and power loom: transformed the textile industry
  • Workers, including children, labored in dangerous factory conditions for low wages

2. Key Inventions

A flood of inventions changed everyday life in the 1800s.

Examples:

  • Telegraph (Samuel Morse, 1844): instant long-distance communication
  • Light bulb (Thomas Edison, 1879): revolutionized life after dark
  • Telephone (Alexander Graham Bell, 1876): voice communication over distance

lessons.title: World Wars and the 20th Century
lessons.content:
World Wars and the 20th Century

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the main causes of WWI and WWII
  • Describe the impact on civilians
  • Understand the formation of the United Nations

1. World War I (1914–1918)

WWI began after the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand and drew in nations worldwide.

Examples:

  • New, deadly weapons: machine guns, poison gas, tanks, airplanes
  • The Western Front: soldiers lived in muddy trenches for years
  • ~17 million deaths; ended with the Treaty of Versailles (1919)

2. World War II (1939–1945)

WWII was the deadliest conflict in human history.

Examples:

  • Nazi Germany, led by Adolf Hitler, invaded neighboring countries and killed 6 million Jews in the Holocaust
  • The U.S. entered after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor (December 7, 1941)
  • Ended with Germany's surrender and U.S. atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki
  • The United Nations was founded in 1945 to promote peace

lessons.title: The Modern World — Rights and Progress
lessons.content:
The Modern World — Rights and Progress

Learning Objectives

  • Describe the global struggle for civil and human rights
  • Explain the women's suffrage and feminist movements
  • Describe how technology has changed daily life

1. Civil Rights Movements

People around the world have fought for equal rights and dignity.

Examples:

  • U.S. Civil Rights Movement: ended legal segregation (Civil Rights Act, 1964)
  • Nelson Mandela fought against apartheid in South Africa; became its first democratically elected president
  • Mahatma Gandhi led nonviolent resistance to British rule in India

2. Women's Rights and Technology

Women fought for and won major rights in the 20th century, while technology transformed the world.

Examples:

  • 19th Amendment (1920): women gain the right to vote in the U.S.
  • Marie Curie: first woman to win a Nobel Prize (and the first person to win two)
  • The Internet (1990s): connected the world and changed communication, commerce, and culture forever

courses.title: History — 3rd Grade
courses.description: World & American history across the ages. Grade level: 3rd Grade.

lessons.title: Prehistoric Humans
lessons.content:
Prehistoric Humans

Learning Objectives

  • Describe the lifestyle of early hunter-gatherers
  • Explain the Neolithic Revolution
  • Identify early tools and artifacts

1. Hunter-Gatherers

For most of human history, people moved in small groups hunting animals and gathering plants.

Examples:

  • Paleolithic ('Old Stone Age'): ~2.5 million–10,000 BCE
  • Made stone tools, wore animal skins, lived in caves or temporary shelters
  • Cave paintings (Lascaux, France): ~17,000 years old — evidence of artistic expression

2. The Neolithic Revolution

About 12,000 years ago, people began farming — one of history's greatest turning points.

Examples:

  • Neolithic ('New Stone Age'): ~10,000–3,000 BCE
  • Settled in permanent villages, domesticated animals, grew crops
  • Freed time for other skills: pottery, weaving, metalworking

lessons.title: Ancient China and India
lessons.content:
Ancient China and India

Learning Objectives

  • Describe the achievements of ancient China (Great Wall, silk, paper)
  • Explain the significance of the Indus Valley Civilization
  • Compare ancient China and India

1. Ancient China

Chinese civilization developed along the Yellow River over 4,000 years ago.

Examples:

  • Four Great Inventions: paper, printing, gunpowder, compass
  • The Silk Road: trade route connecting China to Europe
  • The Great Wall: built over centuries to protect against invasion

2. Indus Valley Civilization

One of the world's earliest civilizations thrived in modern-day Pakistan and India (~2600–1900 BCE).

Examples:

  • Planned cities with grid layouts, advanced drainage systems
  • Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro: major cities with populations of 30,000+
  • Traded with Mesopotamia; had a writing system not yet fully deciphered

lessons.title: Ancient Africa — Egypt and Beyond
lessons.content:
Ancient Africa — Egypt and Beyond

Learning Objectives

  • Name and locate key ancient African kingdoms
  • Describe the wealth and power of the Mali Empire
  • Explain the importance of Timbuktu as a center of learning

1. Kingdoms of Africa

Africa was home to powerful kingdoms with advanced cultures and economies.

Examples:

  • Kingdom of Kush (Nubia): traded gold and ivory with Egypt and Rome
  • Axum (Ethiopia): powerful trading empire; adopted Christianity in the 4th century CE
  • Mali Empire: controlled trans-Saharan gold and salt trade

2. Mansa Musa and Timbuktu

Mali's Emperor Mansa Musa was perhaps the wealthiest person in history.

Examples:

  • His 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca with 60,000 people and tonnes of gold stunned the world
  • Timbuktu: major center of Islamic scholarship with 180 schools and the University of Sankore
  • West African oral tradition preserved history through griots (storytellers)

lessons.title: The Islamic Golden Age
lessons.content:
The Islamic Golden Age

Learning Objectives

  • Explain when and where the Islamic Golden Age occurred
  • Describe achievements in medicine, astronomy, and mathematics
  • Name key scholars and their contributions

1. When and Where

The Islamic Golden Age (8th–13th centuries) centered in Baghdad, the world's largest city at its peak.

Examples:

  • The Abbasid Caliphate built the House of Wisdom — a great library and research center
  • Scholars translated Greek and Roman texts into Arabic, preserving ancient knowledge
  • Baghdad was a cosmopolitan city where Muslims, Christians, and Jews worked together

2. Achievements and Scholars

Islamic scholars made breakthroughs that shaped the modern world.

Examples:

  • Al-Khwarizmi: father of algebra (the word 'algebra' comes from his book Al-Kitab al-mukhtasar)
  • Ibn Sina (Avicenna): The Canon of Medicine — used as a textbook in Europe for 600 years
  • Al-Biruni: mapped the Earth, calculated its circumference accurately

lessons.title: The Aztec and Inca Empires
lessons.content:
The Aztec and Inca Empires

Learning Objectives

  • Describe the location and features of the Aztec Empire
  • Explain how the Incas built their empire in the Andes
  • Compare the two civilizations

1. The Aztec Empire

The Aztecs built one of the Americas' greatest empires in central Mexico.

Examples:

  • Tenochtitlan (modern Mexico City): island city of 200,000+ people — larger than any European city of its time
  • Chinampas: floating gardens that dramatically increased food production
  • The Aztec calendar and writing system were highly sophisticated

2. The Inca Empire

The Incas built the largest empire in pre-Columbian America along the Andes Mountains.

Examples:

  • Machu Picchu: stunning mountain citadel built ~1450 CE
  • 40,000 km of roads connecting the empire; no wheeled vehicles or horses — all on foot
  • The quipu: a system of knotted strings used for record-keeping

lessons.title: The Reformation and Religious Change
lessons.content:
The Reformation and Religious Change

Learning Objectives

  • Explain why Luther challenged the Church
  • Describe the impact of the Reformation
  • Explain how the Reformation changed Europe

1. Martin Luther's Challenge

In 1517, Martin Luther nailed his 95 Theses to a church door in Wittenberg, criticizing corrupt Church practices.

Examples:

  • He objected to 'indulgences' — paying money to the Church to have sins forgiven
  • The printing press spread his ideas rapidly across Europe
  • Luther was excommunicated (expelled) by the Pope

2. Impact of the Reformation

The Reformation split Christianity and changed European politics forever.

Examples:

  • New Protestant denominations formed: Lutheran, Calvinist, Anglican
  • Wars of Religion: countries fought over religious control
  • Increased literacy as people read the Bible in their own language (Luther translated it into German)

lessons.title: Slavery and the Slave Trade
lessons.content:
Slavery and the Slave Trade

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the scale and route of the transatlantic slave trade
  • Describe the Middle Passage and conditions of enslaved people
  • Connect slavery to its long-term legacy

1. The Transatlantic Slave Trade

Between the 16th and 19th centuries, approximately 12.5 million Africans were forcibly taken to the Americas.

Examples:

  • The Triangular Trade: Europe → Africa (goods) → Americas (enslaved people) → Europe (sugar, cotton, tobacco)
  • Enslaved people were stripped of their names, languages, and families
  • Brazil received the most enslaved Africans (~4.9 million); the U.S. received ~400,000

2. Resistance and Abolition

Enslaved people resisted constantly, and abolitionists fought to end the trade.

Examples:

  • Nat Turner's Rebellion (1831): largest U.S. slave revolt
  • Harriet Tubman's Underground Railroad helped ~70 people escape
  • British abolished the slave trade in 1807; the U.S. in 1865 (13th Amendment)

lessons.title: Revolutions — American and French
lessons.content:
Revolutions — American and French

Learning Objectives

  • Identify the causes of each revolution
  • Compare the outcomes
  • Explain the lasting influence of revolutionary ideals

1. Shared Ideals

Both revolutions were inspired by Enlightenment ideas about freedom, equality, and government.

Examples:

  • John Locke: people have natural rights (life, liberty, property) — governments exist to protect them
  • Enlightenment philosophers questioned monarchy and religious authority
  • Both revolutions drew on these ideas to justify overthrowing existing power

2. Outcomes and Legacy

The two revolutions had different paths but lasting global impact.

Examples:

  • American Revolution: stable democratic republic, Constitution, Bill of Rights
  • French Revolution: violent upheaval, Reign of Terror, eventually Napoleon's dictatorship
  • Both inspired later revolutions in Latin America, Europe, and beyond

lessons.title: Colonialism and Its Legacy
lessons.content:
Colonialism and Its Legacy

Learning Objectives

  • Define colonialism and imperialism
  • Describe the 'Scramble for Africa'
  • Explain why colonialism's legacy still affects the world today

1. What Is Colonialism?

Colonialism is when a powerful nation takes control of another territory, exploiting its people and resources.

Examples:

  • European powers colonized most of Africa, Asia, and the Americas from the 15th–20th centuries
  • Motivated by resources (gold, rubber, oil), markets, and the belief in 'civilizing' other peoples
  • The Berlin Conference (1884–85): European powers divided Africa among themselves without African input

2. Legacy of Colonialism

Colonialism created borders, political systems, and inequalities that persist today.

Examples:

  • Artificial borders in Africa split ethnic groups and created lasting conflicts
  • Economic dependence: many former colonies still export raw materials and import manufactured goods
  • Many nations gained independence in the 1950s–70s (decolonization movement)

lessons.title: The Cold War and Modern History
lessons.content:
The Cold War and Modern History

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the ideological conflict between the U.S. and USSR
  • Describe the Space Race and its achievements
  • Identify major events: Berlin Wall, Cuban Missile Crisis, fall of communism

1. The Cold War

After WWII, the U.S. and Soviet Union competed for global influence without direct fighting.

Examples:

  • The arms race: both sides built enough nuclear weapons to destroy the world many times over
  • NATO vs. Warsaw Pact: two competing military alliances
  • Proxy wars: Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan — fighting through other countries

2. Space Race and End of Cold War

Competition extended to space, and eventually communism collapsed in Eastern Europe.

Examples:

  • 1957: Sputnik — first satellite (USSR)
  • 1969: Moon landing — first humans on the Moon (USA)
  • 1989: Berlin Wall falls — Germany reunifies
  • 1991: Soviet Union dissolves — Cold War ends

courses.title: History — 4th Grade
courses.description: World & American history across the ages. Grade level: 4th Grade.

lessons.title: The Ancient World — Overview
lessons.content:
The Ancient World — Overview

Learning Objectives

  • Compare major ancient civilizations
  • Identify common features across early societies
  • Explain how geography shaped civilizations

1. What Civilizations Share

Despite arising independently, ancient civilizations had striking similarities.

Examples:

  • All developed near reliable water sources: Nile, Tigris/Euphrates, Indus, Yellow River
  • All developed writing, organized religion, and specialized labor
  • All created government structures to manage growing populations

2. Geography's Role

The environment shaped what civilizations could build and how they lived.

Examples:

  • River valleys: fertile soil, water for irrigation → farming surpluses → complex societies
  • Natural barriers (mountains, deserts): provided protection or isolated cultures
  • Access to sea: enabled trade and cultural exchange

lessons.title: Democracy and Governance Through Time
lessons.content:
Democracy and Governance Through Time

Learning Objectives

  • Describe Athenian democracy
  • Explain Magna Carta's significance
  • Connect historical governance to modern democracy

1. From Athens to Rome

Democratic governance has ancient roots but has evolved dramatically.

Examples:

  • Athenian direct democracy (~500 BCE): male citizens voted on laws directly
  • Roman Republic: elected Senate and consuls; model for future democracies
  • Julius Caesar's rise showed how democracies can fall to strongmen

2. Magna Carta to Modern Democracy

Key documents and events gradually expanded who had rights.

Examples:

  • Magna Carta (1215): English nobles forced King John to limit royal power
  • English Bill of Rights (1689): Parliament gains power over the monarchy
  • U.S. Constitution (1787) and Bill of Rights (1791): blueprint for modern democracy
  • Universal suffrage expanded slowly: women, Black Americans, and others won voting rights over centuries

lessons.title: The American Civil War in Depth
lessons.content:
The American Civil War in Depth

Learning Objectives

  • Analyze the multiple causes of the Civil War
  • Describe key battles and turning points
  • Evaluate the successes and failures of Reconstruction

1. Causes and Key Battles

The Civil War had economic, political, and moral dimensions.

Examples:

  • Slavery was the central cause, intertwined with states' rights and economic differences
  • Battle of Gettysburg (1863): bloodiest battle; Union victory was a turning point
  • Sherman's March to the Sea (1864): Union destroyed Confederate supply lines

2. Reconstruction (1865–1877)

Reconstruction aimed to rebuild the South and integrate freed Black Americans.

Examples:

  • 13th, 14th, 15th Amendments: abolished slavery, granted citizenship, granted Black men the vote
  • Freedmen's Bureau: provided food, education, and legal help to freed people
  • Compromise of 1877 ended Reconstruction; Southern states enacted Jim Crow laws restricting Black rights

lessons.title: The Progressive Era
lessons.content:
The Progressive Era

Learning Objectives

  • Explain the problems that Progressives sought to fix
  • Name key reformers and their achievements
  • Connect Progressive-era reforms to today

1. Problems of the Gilded Age

Rapid industrialization created enormous wealth but also terrible inequality.

Examples:

  • 'Robber barons' like Rockefeller and Carnegie controlled vast monopolies
  • Workers (including children) labored 12+ hours/day in dangerous factories
  • Urban slums were overcrowded and unsanitary; corruption was rampant

2. Progressive Reforms

Reformers fought to regulate business, protect workers, and expand democracy.

Examples:

  • Theodore Roosevelt: broke up monopolies (antitrust laws), created national parks
  • Jane Addams: Hull House — provided education and social services to immigrants in Chicago
  • 19th Amendment (1920): women win the right to vote (suffrage movement led by Susan B. Anthony, Elizabeth Cady Stanton)

lessons.title: The Great Depression and New Deal
lessons.content:
The Great Depression and New Deal

Learning Objectives

  • Explain causes of the Great Depression
  • Describe its human impact through primary sources
  • Evaluate the New Deal's effectiveness

1. Causes and Impact

The Great Depression began with the stock market crash of 1929 and lasted a decade.

Examples:

  • Banks collapsed; millions lost their life savings overnight
  • Unemployment reached 25%; millions of families lost their homes
  • The Dust Bowl: severe drought devastated Great Plains farms; 2.5 million people fled westward

2. The New Deal

FDR's New Deal used government programs to put people back to work and restore confidence.

Examples:

  • Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC): young men planted trees, built parks
  • Social Security Act (1935): provided pensions for the elderly — still exists today
  • FDIC: insured bank deposits so people wouldn't lose savings if banks failed

lessons.title: World War II — America's Role
lessons.content:
World War II — America's Role

Learning Objectives

  • Explain why the U.S. entered WWII
  • Describe the home front experience (including Japanese American internment)
  • Explain D-Day and the war's end

1. Entering the War

The U.S. entered WWII after Japan's surprise attack on Pearl Harbor, Hawaii.

Examples:

  • December 7, 1941: 'A date which will live in infamy' (FDR)
  • The U.S. fought on two fronts: Europe (against Nazi Germany) and Pacific (against Japan)
  • Over 16 million Americans served in the military during WWII

2. Home Front and Victory

Americans at home played a crucial role in the war effort.

Examples:

  • Rosie the Riveter: women entered factories in record numbers to build weapons
  • Japanese American internment: 120,000 Japanese Americans were forced into camps (a grave injustice)
  • D-Day (June 6, 1944): massive Allied invasion of Normandy, France — turned the tide in Europe
  • August 1945: atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki; Japan surrenders

lessons.title: The Civil Rights Movement in Depth
lessons.content:
The Civil Rights Movement in Depth

Learning Objectives

  • Analyze the philosophy of nonviolent resistance
  • Trace key events from 1954–1968
  • Evaluate the movement's legislative victories and unfinished work

1. Nonviolent Resistance

Inspired by Gandhi, Civil Rights leaders used nonviolent protest to expose injustice.

Examples:

  • Sit-ins: Black students sat at segregated lunch counters and refused to leave
  • Freedom Rides: interracial groups rode buses into the segregated South
  • The March on Washington (1963): 250,000 people heard MLK's 'I Have a Dream' speech

2. Legislative Victories and Legacy

The movement achieved landmark legislation but many challenges remain.

Examples:

  • Brown v. Board of Education (1954): Supreme Court ruled school segregation unconstitutional
  • Civil Rights Act (1964): outlawed discrimination based on race, color, religion, or sex
  • Voting Rights Act (1965): ended discriminatory voting practices
  • Today: movements like Black Lives Matter continue fighting for racial equity

lessons.title: The Vietnam War and Counterculture
lessons.content:
The Vietnam War and Counterculture

Learning Objectives

  • Explain U.S. involvement in Vietnam
  • Describe the antiwar movement
  • Explain the cultural changes of the 1960s–70s

1. The Vietnam War

The U.S. fought in Vietnam from 1955–1975 to prevent the spread of communism.

Examples:

  • U.S. involvement escalated after the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964)
  • Over 58,000 Americans and 2+ million Vietnamese died
  • It was the first war broadcast nightly on TV — shaping public opinion against the war

2. Counterculture and Change

The Vietnam era sparked enormous cultural change in America.

Examples:

  • Antiwar protests on college campuses; Kent State (1970): 4 students killed by National Guard
  • The women's liberation movement gained momentum
  • The environmental movement: first Earth Day (1970), Clean Air Act, EPA established

lessons.title: Late 20th Century — Technology and Globalization
lessons.content:
Late 20th Century — Technology and Globalization

Learning Objectives

  • Define globalization and explain its causes
  • Describe the impact of the digital revolution
  • Evaluate benefits and challenges of a globalized world

1. The Digital Revolution

The invention and spread of computers and the internet transformed every aspect of life.

Examples:

  • 1970s–80s: personal computers became affordable (Apple, IBM)
  • 1991: World Wide Web (Tim Berners-Lee) makes the internet public
  • Social media (Facebook, 2004; Twitter, 2006): changed communication, politics, and society

2. Globalization

Economies and cultures became increasingly interconnected.

Examples:

  • Global trade: your phone is designed in the U.S., made in China, with materials from Africa
  • Multinational corporations operate across dozens of countries
  • Cultural exchange: music, food, film, and fashion spread globally
  • Challenges: inequality between nations, climate change requires global cooperation

lessons.title: The 21st Century — Challenges and Hopes
lessons.content:
The 21st Century — Challenges and Hopes

Learning Objectives

  • Describe key events: 9/11, Great Recession, COVID-19
  • Identify major global challenges
  • Discuss the role students can play in shaping the future

1. 21st Century Events

The new century brought both crises and breakthroughs.

Examples:

  • September 11, 2001: terrorist attacks on the U.S.; led to wars in Afghanistan and Iraq
  • The Great Recession (2008): global financial crisis; millions lost homes and jobs
  • COVID-19 pandemic (2020): global health crisis that changed daily life worldwide

2. Challenges and Your Role

Today's students will shape the solutions to tomorrow's biggest challenges.

Examples:

  • Climate change: rising temperatures, extreme weather, sea level rise
  • Inequality: the gap between rich and poor continues to grow globally
  • Democracy: protecting free elections and human rights around the world
  • You can make history — learn from the past to build a better future

courses.title: Geography — Kindergarten
courses.description: Maps, regions, landforms & world cultures. Grade level: Kindergarten.

lessons.title: Me on the Map
lessons.content:
Me on the Map

Learning Objectives

  • Draw a simple map of a familiar place
  • Understand that maps show places from above
  • Identify a globe as a model of Earth

1. What is a Map?

A map is a drawing of a place as if you were looking at it from above.

Examples:

  • Draw your bedroom from a bird's-eye view
  • Draw your classroom from above
  • A map of your neighborhood would show streets, parks, and buildings

2. Globes and Earth

A globe is a round model of Earth that shows all the land and water.

Examples:

  • Earth has more water (oceans) than land
  • You can spin a globe to see all parts of Earth
  • A flat map stretches the round Earth, but a globe shows true shapes

lessons.title: Land and Water
lessons.content:
Land and Water

Learning Objectives

  • Name basic landforms: mountain, hill, valley, plain, island
  • Name bodies of water: ocean, river, lake, pond
  • Locate land and water on a simple map

1. Landforms

The surface of the Earth has many different shapes.

Examples:

  • Mountain: tall, rocky land
  • Hill: smaller than a mountain, rounded at the top
  • Valley: low land between hills or mountains
  • Plain: flat, wide stretch of land
  • Island: land completely surrounded by water

2. Bodies of Water

Water covers most of Earth's surface in different forms.

Examples:

  • Ocean: the largest body of salt water
  • River: fresh water flowing across land
  • Lake: body of fresh water surrounded by land
  • Pond: small, shallow body of fresh water

lessons.title: Our Neighborhood and Community
lessons.content:
Our Neighborhood and Community

Learning Objectives

  • Define neighborhood and community
  • Identify key places: school, park, library, store
  • Draw a simple map of the neighborhood

1. What's in My Neighborhood?

A neighborhood is the area around where you live, full of places and people.

Examples:

  • School, park, grocery store, post office, fire station
  • Neighborhoods can be urban (city), suburban (near a city), or rural (countryside)

2. Community Helpers and Places

Certain buildings serve the whole community.

Examples:

  • Library: free books and learning for everyone
  • Hospital: medical care for sick or injured people
  • Fire station: firefighters protect the community from fires

lessons.title: Cardinal Directions
lessons.content:
Cardinal Directions

Learning Objectives

  • Name the four cardinal directions
  • Use cardinal directions to describe location
  • Apply directions to a simple map

1. North, South, East, West

The four cardinal directions help us describe where things are located.

Examples:

  • The sun rises in the East and sets in the West
  • On a map, North is usually at the top
  • 'Never Eat Shredded Wheat' — a way to remember N, E, S, W going clockwise

2. Using Directions on a Map

We use a compass rose on maps to show directions.

Examples:

  • The library is north of the school
  • The park is east of the grocery store
  • Turn left (West) at the corner to reach the post office

lessons.title: Our Country — The United States
lessons.content:
Our Country — The United States

Learning Objectives

  • Locate the U.S. on a world map
  • Name a few states and their capitals
  • Describe geographic diversity of the U.S.

1. The United States

The United States is a large country in North America made up of 50 states.

Examples:

  • 50 states, each with its own capital city
  • Washington D.C. is the national capital
  • Bordered by Canada to the north, Mexico to the south, Pacific Ocean to the west, Atlantic Ocean to the east

2. Geographic Diversity

The U.S. has many different landforms and climates.

Examples:

  • Rocky Mountains in the West
  • Great Plains in the Midwest
  • Appalachian Mountains in the East
  • Everglades wetlands in Florida
  • Desert Southwest (Arizona, Nevada)

lessons.title: The Seven Continents
lessons.content:
The Seven Continents

Learning Objectives

  • Name all seven continents
  • Locate continents on a world map
  • Name the four major oceans

1. Seven Continents

Earth's land is divided into seven large areas called continents.

Examples:

  • North America, South America, Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia (Oceania), Antarctica
  • Asia is the largest continent; Australia is the smallest
  • Antarctica has no permanent human population — only scientists visit

2. Four Oceans

Earth's oceans cover about 71% of the surface.

Examples:

  • Pacific (largest), Atlantic, Indian, Arctic
  • The Pacific Ocean is larger than all land on Earth combined
  • Oceans connect all continents and are vital for weather and climate

lessons.title: Weather and Climate Around the World
lessons.content:
Weather and Climate Around the World

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish between weather and climate
  • Explain why different places have different climates
  • Match climates to regions of the world

1. Hot, Cold, and In Between

Different parts of the world have very different climates.

Examples:

  • Near the equator: hot and sunny all year (tropics)
  • Near the poles: cold and icy most of the year
  • In between: four seasons — warm summers and cold winters

2. Climate Zones

Scientists divide the world into three main climate zones.

Examples:

  • Tropical: near the equator — Amazon Rainforest, Central Africa
  • Temperate: mid-latitudes — the U.S., Europe, China
  • Polar: near the poles — Arctic, Antarctica, northern Canada

lessons.title: People and Places — How We Adapt
lessons.content:
People and Places — How We Adapt

Learning Objectives

  • Give examples of how people adapt to cold climates
  • Give examples of adapting to hot or dry climates
  • Explain why houses look different around the world

1. Adapting to Cold

People in cold climates design their lives around staying warm.

Examples:

  • Thick insulated homes; underfloor heating in Scandinavia
  • Inuit igloos: ice traps body heat and keeps interior warm
  • Heavy clothing, dog sleds, snowshoes

2. Adapting to Heat and Dryness

People in hot or dry climates focus on staying cool and finding water.

Examples:

  • Desert homes: thick walls keep interiors cool during hot days
  • Nomadic lifestyles: following water and grazing land (Bedouin, Masai)
  • Shade structures, light-colored clothing, water storage systems

lessons.title: Maps and Map Skills
lessons.content:
Maps and Map Skills

Learning Objectives

  • Read a map legend/key
  • Understand that map symbols represent real things
  • Use a simple scale to estimate distance

1. Map Legends and Symbols

A map legend (or key) explains what the symbols on a map mean.

Examples:

  • A blue line might represent a river
  • A green area might represent a park or forest
  • A star symbol usually marks a capital city

2. Map Scale

A map scale shows the relationship between distance on the map and real distance.

Examples:

  • 1 inch = 10 miles: two cities 3 inches apart are about 30 miles apart in real life
  • A world map has a very small scale (large area, small map)
  • A neighborhood map has a large scale (small area, big map)

lessons.title: Our Planet — Caring for Earth
lessons.content:
Our Planet — Caring for Earth

Learning Objectives

  • Explain how human activities affect geography
  • Identify environmental challenges: deforestation, pollution, water scarcity
  • Describe actions children can take to care for Earth

1. How Humans Change the Land

As populations grow, humans transform the natural landscape.

Examples:

  • Forests cleared for farmland and cities
  • Rivers dammed for electricity and water supply
  • Wetlands drained for development (losing important habitats)

2. Being Earth Stewards

Everyone can help protect Earth's geography.

Examples:

  • Plant trees and native plants to restore habitats
  • Reduce, reuse, recycle to cut down on pollution
  • Use water wisely — millions of people lack clean drinking water
  • Support national parks and conservation areas

courses.title: Geography — 1st Grade
courses.description: Maps, regions, landforms & world cultures. Grade level: 1st Grade.

lessons.title: Maps, Globes, and Geographic Tools
lessons.content:
Maps, Globes, and Geographic Tools

Learning Objectives

  • Read a compass rose with cardinal and intermediate directions
  • Use a grid system to find locations
  • Interpret a map legend with multiple symbols

1. Compass Rose and Grid

A compass rose shows eight directions: N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW.

Examples:

  • NE is between North and East (northeast)
  • Grid systems use letters and numbers to pinpoint locations on a map
  • Find the library: Row C, Column 4 on a classroom map grid

2. Map Legends and Scale

Every good map has a legend and a scale.

Examples:

  • Legend: ★ = capital city, 🌲 = forest, 〰 = river
  • Scale: 1 cm = 50 km — use a ruler to estimate real distances
  • Physical maps show terrain; political maps show borders and cities

lessons.title: Regions of the United States
lessons.content:
Regions of the United States

Learning Objectives

  • Name the five U.S. regions
  • Describe key physical features of each
  • Connect regional geography to economy and culture

1. Five Regions

The U.S. is often divided into five geographic and cultural regions.

Examples:

  • Northeast: oldest settlements, dense cities (New York, Boston), Appalachian Mountains
  • Southeast: warm climate, coastal plains, Everglades, Gulf Coast
  • Midwest: Great Plains, farming ('breadbasket of America'), Great Lakes
  • Southwest: desert, canyons, Hispanic/Native American cultural influence
  • West: Rocky Mountains, Pacific Coast, diverse climates

lessons.title: North America — Continent Study
lessons.content:
North America — Continent Study

Learning Objectives

  • Locate and name key countries, rivers, and landforms
  • Describe North America's climate diversity
  • Explain how the physical geography affects the people

1. Physical Features

North America has incredibly diverse physical geography.

Examples:

  • Rocky Mountains (west), Appalachians (east), Great Plains (center)
  • Mississippi River: longest river in North America (3,730 km)
  • Great Lakes: world's largest group of freshwater lakes
  • Caribbean islands, Central American rainforests, Arctic tundra

2. Countries and People

North America includes 23 countries with diverse cultures and economies.

Examples:

  • U.S.: world's largest economy, huge cultural diversity
  • Canada: second largest country by area; bilingual (English and French)
  • Mexico: rich history (Aztec, Mayan), largest Spanish-speaking country by population

lessons.title: South America — Continent Study
lessons.content:
South America — Continent Study

Learning Objectives

  • Locate key South American countries, rivers, and landforms
  • Describe the Amazon rainforest and its global importance
  • Describe the diversity of South American cultures

1. Physical Features

South America has dramatic geography.

Examples:

  • Andes Mountains: world's longest mountain range (7,000 km along the west coast)
  • Amazon River: largest river by water volume in the world
  • Amazon Rainforest: covers 5.5 million km²; home to 10% of all species on Earth
  • Atacama Desert: driest place on Earth; some areas have never had recorded rain

2. Cultures and Countries

South America has 12 countries with rich cultural diversity.

Examples:

  • Brazil: largest country; Portuguese language; Amazon, Atlantic Forest, Carnival
  • Peru: home of Machu Picchu and the Inca legacy; diverse climate zones (coast, highlands, jungle)
  • Argentina: Patagonia glaciers, Pampas grasslands, tango culture

lessons.title: Europe — Continent Study
lessons.content:
Europe — Continent Study

Learning Objectives

  • Locate key European countries and capitals
  • Describe major landforms and rivers
  • Explain how Europe's geography shaped its history

1. Physical Features

Europe is a relatively small but geographically diverse continent.

Examples:

  • Alps: major mountain range through France, Switzerland, Italy, Austria
  • Rhine, Danube, Thames: major rivers that shaped trade and cities
  • Mediterranean Sea: warm, mild climate in southern Europe; center of ancient civilizations
  • North European Plain: fertile farmland stretching from France to Russia

2. Countries and Culture

Europe has 44 countries, many languages, and shared cultural roots.

Examples:

  • France: Paris, Eiffel Tower, major influence on art and cuisine
  • Germany: largest economy in Europe; industrial powerhouse
  • Italy: birthplace of the Roman Empire and Renaissance
  • Greece: birthplace of democracy and Western philosophy
  • United Kingdom: London, constitutional monarchy, English language

lessons.title: Africa — Continent Study
lessons.content:
Africa — Continent Study

Learning Objectives

  • Locate major African countries, deserts, rivers, and mountains
  • Describe Africa's geographic diversity
  • Appreciate the cultural richness of the African continent

1. Physical Features

Africa is the second largest continent with incredible geographic variety.

Examples:

  • Sahara Desert: world's largest hot desert (9.2 million km²)
  • Nile River: world's longest river (6,650 km), flows through Egypt
  • Congo Rainforest: world's second largest rainforest after the Amazon
  • Kilimanjaro: Africa's highest mountain (5,895 m) in Tanzania
